lesson.title: Reading the Static: What Residual Patterns Reveal
lesson.summary: The shape of a residual plot, not just its individual values, tells you whether a linear model actually fits the data or whether the true relationship bends, fans out, or otherwise breaks the straight-line assumption.
lesson.body:
A residual plot is only useful if you know how to read it. The single most important skill is distinguishing random scatter from a pattern. When a residual plot shows points bouncing above and below zero with no discernible trend, no curve, and no change in spread as x increases, that randomness is good news: it means a straight line, the linear form, is capturing the real structure of the relationship, and whatever is left over is just noise. When a residual plot instead shows a systematic shape, that shape is telling you the linear model is missing something.

The clearest warning sign is curvature. Recall the y = x-squared example: fitting a straight line to the points (1,1), (2,4), (3,9), (4,16), (5,25) produced residuals of 2, -1, -2, -1, 2. Plotted against x, these trace a U-shape, negative in the middle and positive at both ends. This happens precisely because the true relationship curves upward faster than any straight line can track: the best-fit straight line sits above the true curve through the middle of the data and below it at the two extremes, so the line overestimates y in the middle, producing negative residuals there, and underestimates y at the low and high ends, producing positive residuals there. Whenever a residual plot bows up, bows down, or snakes in a clear curve, the message is the same: the relationship is not linear, even if the original scatterplot looked deceptively straight, and the linear form assumed by the regression line is the wrong tool here.

A second common pattern is a fan or funnel shape, where residuals stay small for low x-values and spread increasingly wide for high x-values (or vice versa). This signals that the variability in y is not constant across the range of x, a condition statisticians call unequal variance. A residual plot can show this even when there is no curvature at all, so it is a separate check from the curvature check, not a replacement for it.

It is worth being explicit about what a "good" residual plot looks like, because students often expect residuals to look impressively small rather than impressively random. A residual plot with moderately sized but patternless scatter is a healthy sign; a residual plot with tiny residuals that nonetheless trace a visible curve is a warning sign. Size answers "how far off," while pattern answers "was a straight line even the right shape to fit." The two questions are independent, and interpreting residuals is fundamentally about answering the second one: does the leftover variation look like pure noise, or does it still contain structure that a straight line failed to capture?

Learning to read these shapes turns the residual plot from a piece of arithmetic busywork into the single best diagnostic tool available for checking whether the linear form was ever the right choice in the first place, before any further conclusions are drawn from the regression.
